One user says they liked Unity a lot, probably more than GNOME. They dislike most of Canonical's in-house projects (snaps, upstart, Mir) but wish Canonical had kept Unity.

Unity felt consistent, usable and boring, which this user values in a desktop. They were sad Canonical dropped it, because it set Ubuntu apart and was pretty stable and solid by the time of the switch.
Called Unity probably the most n00b-friendly Linux DE. The user still runs it in 2022 on an old Ubuntu image and finds it less objectionable than GNOME and less fiddly than KDE.
One user disliked Unity at first because of the global menu and top-left close button. After using macOS for a while they came to prefer those ideas, and Unity became one of their favorite desktops.
"I remember quitting Ubuntu because they dropped unity - hah."
For this user, Unity's killer feature was the HUD: you just type to find menu items, which saves a lot of time compared with digging through options.

When Ubuntu moved to GNOME Shell with its customizations, it felt strange for a couple of hours, then everything made sense. The user forgot they weren't using Unity because the icons are where they used to be.

Unity's global menu used vertical space so well that switching to GNOME felt like going back 10 years. Multiple empty bars and random icons replacing menus made it unusable for this user, who moved to KDE Plasma with a global menu, which is good but not as hassle-free.
This user loves Unity and keeps installing it on their desktops; it's now running on 22.04. They feel a lot of thought went into many of its parts.
Unity was OK once the global menu was disabled. The user now runs KDE because it lets them configure things the way they want.
One user never understood Unity and never considered GNOME, KDE or Cinnamon inferior to it. In their view, GNOME implemented and then surpassed any of Unity's claimed features long ago.

After a couple of years on Ubuntu/Compiz, this user reports annoying quirks such as child windows popping up on the wrong monitor (worked around with Win+Shift+arrow keys). Still, they have no desire to go back to Windows 10/8.

Used Compiz with Ubuntu 17.04 and liked it, but tried the native GNOME after a clean 18.04 install: "it's not perfect but it does the job," and they'll stick with it rather than run unmaintained software.

GNOME 2 on early Ubuntu was the complete, reliable, configurable desktop Linux needed, and things went downhill afterwards. GNOME Classic in Ubuntu is okay-ish but has leaky abstractions and takes tweaking to keep long-held keybindings.

On Dell's Ubuntu gaming desktop, one user wants better video drivers, dual-boot, more games and removal of the "painful Unity interface." They cite hiding, unhiding and switching between hidden windows as a pain point.

This user's one wish: typing "calc" in the Dash ranks LibreOffice Calc above the Calculator app, even if Calc has never been used. So they always have to select Calculator manually instead of just pressing Enter.
Left Ubuntu because of bloatware and opinionated choices, and because it crashed a lot. They prefer Antergos with i3-gnome for much better performance and fewer crashes and bugs.
"I'm using the latest Ubuntu GNOME, and I can say that I'm pleased with how it is." They believe using GNOME's own apps where available is better.
Most users say Ubuntu's current default apps (Firefox, Thunderbird, gnome-terminal, Nautilus, Gedit, Evince, LibreOffice) more than suffice. One user's only wish is no change without a good reason.
"Ubuntu works for me and my wife and has for years." They miss GNOME 2 and wish Unity could be made to work like it.
